motion: Is secular humanism better for society than Christianity?

bridges.description: Show that secular humanism better serves human flourishing in this life through human-centered, publicly assessable aims.
Connect revisability, evidence, and open debate to correcting practices when better consequences are found.
Ground equal status, autonomy, and cooperative rights in shared human conditions and collective protection.
Challenge Christianity to connect its theological claims to demonstrable present social benefits.
Show that mere Christianity better cultivates shared values of humility, nobility, solidarity, and hopeful action.
Connect the image of God to species-wide worth independent of capacities or subjective valuation.
Connect emulation of Jesus, care for marginalized people, grace, and nonviolence to present human flourishing.
Challenge humanism to explain rights and moral status beyond changing collective recognition or self-valuation.

sections.title: Frameworks for present human flourishing
sections.rationale: Defines the motion, its present-life scope, and each framework's claimed contribution to flourishing.

sections.title: Revision, public reasons, and practical guidance
sections.rationale: Compares how the frameworks identify, communicate, and correct practical social guidance.

sections.title: Human worth and equal status
sections.rationale: Addresses species-wide worth, capacities, self-valuation, and theological grounding.

sections.title: Moral intuition and warrant
sections.rationale: Examines whether intuitions are tested, justified, properly basic, fallible, and coherent with wider beliefs.

sections.title: Rights, entitlement, and codification
sections.rationale: Distinguishes moral entitlement from the legal creation, recognition, and protection of rights.

sections.title: Equality and the limits of revision
sections.rationale: Tests whether empirically revisable humanism can remain logically committed to equal treatment.

sections.title: Solidarity, self-denial, and hope
sections.rationale: Compares cooperative concern, Christian discipleship, and hope-directed action.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: The comparison should concern human flourishing in this life rather than benefits in an unverified afterlife.
moves.warrant: Secular humanism treats supernatural claims as unavailable for solving shared earthly problems and centers the lives people demonstrably share.
moves.inference: A framework aimed directly at present human welfare has the relevant focus for deciding what is better for society.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Dillahunty's explicit motion framing and ends after the shared-world premise that supports the present-life standard.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm talking about for humans in this life.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous opening statement after the host has yielded the floor to Dillahunty.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification needed; the selected span is a continuous, clearly introduced single-speaker opening turn.
moves.importanceRationale: Sets the motion-level criterion and time horizon used throughout his case.

burdenContact.rationale: Defines the relevant social benefit as present human flourishing.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Humanism can incorporate demonstrably beneficial practices from any source and revise itself when better methods are found.
moves.warrant: It is not a fixed list of commandments; its stated aim permits adoption of what improves human life, using observation, discussion, debate, and evidence.
moves.inference: Its flexibility gives it a corrective mechanism for improving social guidance.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures the complete adoption-and-revision argument through its contrast between evidence-based acceptance and conversion or coercion.
moves.attributionRationale: Uninterrupted portion of Dillahunty's opening statement.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification needed; speaker continuity is explicit and no handoff occurs.
moves.importanceRationale: Supplies a central comparative mechanism by which humanism is claimed to improve.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects openness to evidence with correction of social practices.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Human beings must make ethical decisions together about equality, property, bodily sovereignty, and life purposes without treating human focus as worship.
moves.warrant: People share a world and their choices affect one another, so human-centered deliberation is necessary regardless of theological claims.
moves.inference: A framework that directly protects equal human standing and autonomy is better aligned with the motion.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts at the contrast between human flourishing and God-centered purposes and ends after the full list of concrete autonomy and equality questions.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous single-speaker opening passage.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification needed; the host does not enter until after this selected passage.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Individual freedom should be constrained by its effects on others and assessed by the world produced if people were generally free to act that way.
moves.warrant: People share social space, and broader happiness, health, and autonomy require considering reciprocal impacts.
moves.inference: Humanism supplies a practical cooperative test for conduct that promotes social flourishing.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers the full move from shared-space limits on liberty through the generalization test and its stated social outcome.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Dillahunty opening statement before his next comparative argument.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification needed; the passage has clear first-person continuity.
moves.importanceRationale: Provides a practical subsidiary rule connecting autonomy with responsibility to others.

burdenContact.rationale: Offers a consequence-sensitive method for choosing socially beneficial conduct.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Christianity lacks an agreed method for resolving divergent divine commands and directs resources toward unverified otherworldly aims.
moves.warrant: Christian denominations disagree across social questions, while Dillahunty characterizes Christianity's primary focus as serving and glorifying God rather than present human interests.
moves.inference: That disagreement and shifted focus weaken Christianity as practical guidance for improving this world.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with the concession that Christianity has had positive effects and retains the disagreement and God-centered purpose comparison while stopping exactly at the excluded transition boundary.
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty remains the sole speaker until the excluded mixed event immediately after this span.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification needed; the boundary conservatively excludes the rolling-caption handoff at zero-based event 328.
moves.importanceRationale: Directly compares the rival framework's practical guidance and social focus.

burdenContact.rationale: Demands an accessible way to resolve Christian disagreement and show present benefit.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Christianity overlaps with humanism in humility, human nobility, solidarity, and concern for flourishing.
moves.warrant: Rauser connects Christian mortality, creation in God's image, love of neighbor, and care for the least to the same values he draws from Carl Sagan.
moves.inference: The comparison should ask which framework better cultivates shared pro-social values rather than treating them as opposed in every respect.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts with Rauser's summary of the humanist values and includes his complete Christian parallels and explicit shared-overlap conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Christianity and humanism are not scorched earth enemies.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous opening statement by Rauser after his introduction.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification needed; there is no speaker transition within the span.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: The relevant Christian case is mere Christianity centered on the Apostles Creed and discipleship, not every historical Christian expression.
moves.warrant: Rauser concedes that many Christians and historical forms have failed to cultivate pro-social goods and can perform worse than humanists.
moves.inference: Failures of adherents do not by themselves settle whether his specified Christian framework better supports flourishing.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Rauser's motion framing, his explicit concession about failed Christian practice, and his precise qualification of the Christianity he defends.
moves.attributionRationale: Uninterrupted opening statement with explicit first-person framing.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification needed; the source contains no handoff in this span.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Original sin provides a sober account of persistent individual and collective moral failure rather than moral fatalism.
moves.warrant: Even advanced societies can commit atrocities, and people should recognize their own capacity for grave wrongdoing.
moves.inference: Christianity can cultivate humility and vigilance about moral self-deception in social life.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures the definition of original sin, the historical illustration as presented, and Rauser's explicit non-fatalist conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser is clearly the speaker, but the span contains caption-corrupted proper names and a reported quotation.

moves.importanceRationale: Supports the humility component of his comparative framework but is not alone motion-determinative.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: The image of God grounds value across the entire human species independently of developed capacities.
moves.warrant: Capacity-based accounts risk marginalizing people who do not actualize reason, language, or self-consciousness; the divine-image relation is compared to a provenance mark conferring value.
moves.inference: Christianity offers a more inclusive foundation for human worth.

moves.warrant: Rauser cites the Beatitudes, enemy-love, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s application of nonviolent resistance as a disciplined response to oppression.
moves.inference: Christian discipleship can cultivate socially transformative solidarity.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects emulation of Jesus to concrete solidarity and nonviolent action.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser

moves.warrant: The promised restoration of creation is presented alongside calls to persist in doing good and a broad program of practical service.
